summaries.example: Imagine seeing a stick in water. It may look bent even though it is straight. Medieval thinkers asked whether this kind of mistake means that all seeing is unreliable. Some answered that we can check with touch, careful thinking, or other kinds of knowledge. Others explored how difficult it is to be completely certain.
summaries.summary: Medieval skepticism was about hard questions concerning knowledge. Skeptics wondered whether sight, hearing, memory, and reasoning always tell us the truth. The medieval period did not have one large skeptical movement, but many philosophers discussed these worries. They learned about older Greek and Roman forms of skepticism, especially Academic Skepticism, which said people might have to live by what seems believable rather than by truth that they cannot know. Augustine argued against this view. He said that some things, such as simple mathematics, rules of logic, and the fact that a person is thinking or alive, are secure even when the senses may fool us. Later thinkers in Christian, Islamic, and Jewish settings considered different problems, including optical illusions, dreams, causes, and whether God’s power could make human experiences deceptive. Their answers differed. Some trusted ordinary ways of knowing, while others demanded a very high level of proof. The entry’s main lesson is that medieval skepticism was a set of connected debates, not a single school. These debates made philosophers examine how knowledge works and influenced later philosophy.
key_ideas: Medieval skepticism was not one organized group. It was a collection of questions and replies about knowledge.
Some ancient skeptics doubted that people could know the truth and tried to live peacefully by putting beliefs on hold.
Augustine argued that some truths, including mathematical, logical, and self-related truths, cannot be doubted in the same way as sensory experiences.
Medieval philosophers studied dreams, mistakes by the senses, and the possibility that an all-powerful God could allow people to be deceived.
These debates helped shape later discussions of knowledge, including ideas that appeared again in early modern philosophy.
summaries.why_it_matters: Skepticism teaches us to separate a guess from good knowledge. It encourages careful checking without saying that every question has the same answer. Medieval thinkers also show that people from different intellectual and religious traditions asked related questions about mistakes, proof, and certainty. Thinking about their arguments can help us understand why we trust our senses, our memories, mathematics, and our own thoughts.

important_terms.definition: Skepticism is the view, or a questioning attitude, that asks whether people can really know things for certain.
A skeptic is someone who questions whether a belief is truly known.
Certainty means being completely sure that something is true and cannot be mistaken about it.
An illusion is an experience that seems one way but may not match how things really are.
Self-knowledge is knowing something about your own thoughts or experiences, such as knowing that you are thinking.

questions_to_think_about: Can a mistake in one experience show that every experience is mistaken?
What do you know about your own thoughts that would be hard to doubt?
Why might checking something in more than one way help?
Could someone live normally while doubting everything?

summaries.example: Suppose a person sees a straight stick partly under water and judges that it is bent. A skeptic may argue that if perception can mislead us in this case, perhaps perceptual experience never guarantees knowledge of the external world. A medieval anti-skeptical response might appeal to agreement among different senses, intellectual principles, or the reliability of ordinary cognitive processes. The example does not settle the dispute: it shows why the standard for certainty matters.
summaries.summary: The medieval history of skepticism is best understood not as the survival of a single school but as a changing set of epistemological problems. Ancient sources supplied two important models. Pyrrhonian skeptics opposed competing arguments and suspended judgment in the hope of tranquility. Academic skeptics rejected knowledge of truth while permitting practical reliance on what appeared plausible. In the Latin Middle Ages, Academic materials—especially through Cicero and Augustine—were generally more influential, while Pyrrhonian texts were not widely available. Augustine’s anti-skeptical strategy included claims that doubting itself reveals a thinker’s existence, and that logical and mathematical truths do not depend on secure knowledge of external objects. He also defended a theory of divine illumination. Islamic philosophers contributed important discussions of perception and certainty. Al-Haytham analyzed perception as sometimes inferential and used optical illusions to clarify how error is possible. Al-Ghazali considered doubts arising from disagreement, the senses, reason, and dreams, and described certainty as restored through divine illumination; he also questioned whether observation alone establishes necessary causal connections. In thirteenth- and fourteenth-century scholasticism, debates became increasingly technical. Henry of Ghent grounded full certainty in divine ideas, while Scotus criticized that strategy and defended several kinds of naturally acquired certainty. Auriol, Ockham, and Wodeham examined cognition and perceptual error in different ways. Autrecourt developed an especially radical skepticism, while Buridan accepted some self-evident principles and a weaker standard for empirical knowledge. The result was a diverse medieval background for later
key_ideas: Medieval skepticism was not a continuous movement. It consisted of recurring skeptical problems and anti-skeptical responses across several traditions.
Academic Skepticism was more influential in the Latin medieval world than Pyrrhonian Skepticism, partly because the relevant texts circulated unevenly.
Augustine attacked the claims that nothing can be known and that skepticism produces wisdom and tranquility, while defending logical, mathematical, and self-directed certainties.
Al-Ghazali used doubts about disagreement, sense perception, reason, and dreams in a search for certainty, then located the recovery of certainty in divine illumination rather than a formal proof.
From the thirteenth century onward, university debates examined perception, cognition, causation, induction, and the possibility of divine deception.
Thinkers such as Henry of Ghent, Scotus, Ockham, Wodeham, Autrecourt, and Buridan disagreed about how much certainty human cognition can provide.
summaries.why_it_matters: These debates clarify that skepticism is not simply a refusal to think or believe. It can be a method for testing what counts as evidence, what kind of error is possible, and whether certainty is required for knowledge. Medieval discussions also complicate the familiar story that skepticism vanished after antiquity and reappeared only in early modern philosophy. They show how questions about perception, causation, self-knowledge, and divine power were already being developed in sophisticated ways.

important_terms.definition: Skepticism is a position that challenges whether knowledge is possible, sometimes globally and sometimes only in a particular area.
Academic Skepticism, associated with Plato’s Academy and known especially through Cicero, held that truth may not be knowable while allowing action based on what is plausible.
Pyrrhonian Skepticism used opposing arguments to suspend judgment, aiming at tranquility; it was more radical about doubting claims than the practical Academic approach.
Epochē is suspension of belief or judgment when a person lacks a sufficient basis for deciding that a claim is true.
Global skepticism questions whether knowledge is possible at all, whereas local skepticism targets a particular source or kind of knowledge.
Divine illumination is the Augustinian idea that certainty depends on access to divine ideas or light rather than on sensory experience alone.
Intuitive cognition concerns something as present and existing; abstractive cognition concerns it from a remove, such as in memory or inference.
The principle of non-contradiction says that the same thing cannot both be and not be in the same respect.

questions_to_think_about: Is living by what is plausible a satisfactory response to the claim that truth cannot be known?
Does the possibility of sensory error undermine all perceptual knowledge, or only some judgments?
Why might the possibility of divine deception create a special problem for a theistic theory of knowledge?
Can knowledge of one’s own thinking survive radical doubt about the external world?
What is gained, and what is lost, when a philosopher lowers the standard from absolute certainty to conditional or probable evidence?

summaries.example: You are sure that your friend is standing across the playground because you see them. Then you remember that a costume or a shadow has fooled you before. Does that mean you cannot know your friend is there? Some medieval philosophers said one mistaken sense experience does not destroy every reliable experience. They might also ask whether another sense, such as hearing or touch, supports what you see. A skeptic would press further: how do you know which check is trustworthy?
summaries.summary: Medieval skepticism explored whether human beings can know the world, themselves, and general truths. It was not a single movement with one leader or one official doctrine. Instead, philosophers in Christian, Islamic, and Jewish intellectual settings discussed problems inherited from ancient philosophy and problems that developed in their own period. Two ancient traditions mattered especially. Pyrrhonian skeptics tried to suspend judgment when arguments seemed evenly matched. Academic skeptics also doubted that truth could be known, but they thought people could guide their lives by what appeared plausible. Augustine was one of the most important medieval critics of skepticism. He argued that a person who doubts still knows that they are doubting, thinking, or alive. He also defended mathematical and logical truths as knowledge that does not require certainty about physical objects. Other thinkers focused on perception. Al-Haytham explained that some perceptions involve fast mental inferences, which helps explain why errors and optical illusions occur. Al-Ghazali examined disagreement, misleading appearances, dreams, and the possibility that even reasoning might fail. He described certainty as returning through divine illumination, not through a chain of ordinary proofs alone. In the universities of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, philosophers developed more detailed accounts of cognition and evidence. Henry of Ghent connected complete certainty with divine ideas. Scotus challenged parts of that view and defended several kinds of knowledge from logic, experience, and the senses. key_ideas: The Middle Ages did not have one team of skeptics. Philosophers in different places raised skeptical worries and tried different answers.
Ancient Pyrrhonian and Academic skepticism were important sources, but medieval readers often knew Academic skepticism better and sometimes mixed the two traditions together.
Augustine argued that doubting does not erase all knowledge. A person can know that they are doubting, and some logical and mathematical truths do not depend on seeing the outside world.
Al-Haytham’s study of perception showed how people may make quick, unnoticed inferences and mistakes when they see things.
Al-Ghazali questioned the senses, reasoning, and ordinary ideas about causes while seeking knowledge that could not be mistaken.
Later university philosophers debated whether certainty comes from divine help, stable features of things, reliable senses, reasoning, or experience.
summaries.why_it_matters: Medieval skepticism matters because it reveals how carefully philosophers have examined everyday knowledge. Seeing, remembering, reasoning, and learning from experience can all seem ordinary until someone asks how they justify belief. The medieval debates also connect ancient skepticism with later philosophy, while showing that medieval thinkers added distinctive questions about divine power, cognition, and self-knowledge. Studying these disagreements helps us compare different standards for what counts as knowing.

important_terms.definition: Skepticism is careful questioning about whether people can know something, especially whether they can be completely certain.
Academic Skepticism was an ancient approach that doubted whether truth could be known but allowed people to act on what seemed reasonable or likely.
Pyrrhonian Skepticism was a more radical approach that used competing arguments to suspend judgment instead of claiming certainty.
Suspension of judgment means refusing to decide that a claim is true or false when the evidence does not settle the matter.
Global skepticism questions whether any knowledge is possible; local skepticism questions only one area, such as what the senses tell us.
Divine illumination is the view that God helps make certain knowledge possible through divine truth or ideas.
An optical illusion is a visual experience that does not accurately show the object or event being observed.
The principle of non-contradiction says that a statement and its opposite cannot both be true in the same way at the same time.

questions_to_think_about: If one sense makes a mistake, should we distrust all the senses?
Is it possible to act sensibly without being certain?
Why might a dream make someone question waking experience?
What kinds of facts seem easier to know: facts about your own thoughts, mathematics, or distant physical objects?
Should knowledge require perfect certainty, or can strong but fallible evidence be enough?
